chapters.title: Chapter 4: Currencies, Commodities and Managing Risk

lessons.title: Hedging in Plain Language: Forwards, Futures and Options for Businesses

children.text: The last two lessons showed how currency and commodity moves hit a business through no fault of anyone working in it. This lesson covers what companies do about it. Hedging has a reputation for being complicated and slightly dangerous. The instruments are actually simple; what gets companies into trouble is using them without a policy.

body.text: Hedging is not about winning. It is about buying certainty so that the business is judged on how well it operates, not on where the rupee happened to close. A hedge that loses money while the business stays predictable has done its job.

children.text: Three Instruments, One Purpose

markDefs.definition: Taking a position that offsets an existing business exposure, so that a loss on one side is balanced by a gain on the other.
A privately agreed contract to buy or sell a specified amount of currency or commodity on a future date at a rate fixed today. Usually arranged with a bank and tailored to the exact amount and date.
The amount paid upfront to buy an option. It is the maximum the buyer can lose, and it is non-refundable whether the option is used or not.

body.text: Always look for the natural hedge first. An IT company that earns in dollars and opens a development centre abroad has reduced its exposure without buying a single contract. A company that invoices its customers in the same currency it pays its suppliers has done the same. The cheapest hedge is the one you never have to transact.

children.text: A Forward, Worked Through All Three Outcomes

An importer must pay USD 1 million in three months. The spot rate today is ₹84. The bank quotes a three-month forward at ₹85.20, which is higher because Indian interest rates are higher than dollar rates, and that difference gets built into every forward quote. The company books the forward, fixing its cost at ₹8.52 crore.

children.text: That third row is the one that gets treasury teams criticised in review meetings, and it should not. The company did not lose ₹32 lakh; it paid ₹32 lakh for three months of certainty and then found out, after the fact, that it did not need it. That is the same logic as insurance on a factory that did not burn down.

body.label: What a Forward Costs
body.context: A forward removes the risk of the rate going against you and also removes the benefit of it moving in your favour. There is no version of this where you keep only the good half for free.

children.text: Options: Paying to Keep the Good Half

The same importer could instead buy a call option on the dollar at a strike of ₹85, paying a premium of ₹1.20 per dollar. On USD 1 million that premium costs ₹12 lakh, paid now and gone whatever happens. What it buys is a ceiling on the rate, with the freedom to walk away if the rupee strengthens.

body.caption: A bought call on the dollar: losses are capped at the premium of ₹1.20 per dollar, while protection continues however high the rate goes above the ₹85 strike.

body.title: The Worst It Can Get
body.prompt: An importer buys a call option on the dollar with a strike of ₹85 and pays a premium of ₹1.20 per dollar. What is the effective worst-case rate it will pay, in ₹ per dollar?
body.explanation: ₹85 strike plus ₹1.20 premium = ₹86.20. However far the rupee falls, the importer cannot pay more than this in effective terms. Compare that with the forward at ₹85.20: the option is one rupee worse in the bad case, and that extra rupee is what buys the right to benefit if the rupee strengthens instead.

columns.label: Forward at ₹85.20
points: Cost is fixed at ₹8.52 crore, whatever happens
No benefit if the rupee strengthens to ₹82
Simple to book and to explain to a board
Must be honoured even if the underlying deal falls through

columns.label: Call Option at ₹85 Strike
points: ₹12 lakh premium paid upfront and unrecoverable
Worst case is ₹86.20, so protection is slightly costlier
Full benefit if the rupee strengthens, less the premium
Needs more explanation, and the premium looks wasted in hindsight
Can simply be abandoned if the underlying deal disappears

body.title: The Tender You Might Not Win
body.question: Your company has bid for an export order worth USD 3 million. You will know in two months whether you won, and payment would follow six months later. Which hedge fits this situation best?
options: A forward contract for the full USD 3 million now
An option, so that protection lapses harmlessly if you lose the bid
No hedge at all, since the exposure is uncertain
A futures contract for double the amount, to be safe
body.explanation: This is a contingent exposure: it may never exist. A forward would still have to be honoured even if you lose the bid, leaving you with a currency position and no underlying business, which is speculation by accident. An option costs a premium but simply lapses if the bid fails. The last choice, hedging twice the exposure, is not caution at all; it creates a position larger than the risk being managed.

body.text: A hedge larger than the underlying exposure is not a hedge. It is a trade. Several Indian companies have booked large losses on currency and commodity derivatives precisely because positions grew beyond the exposures they were meant to protect, often with structures nobody outside treasury fully understood. If an instrument cannot be explained in two sentences to a non-finance director, that is information in itself.

body.title: What a Sensible Hedging Policy Contains

children.text: Companies that use derivatives well tend to have a short written policy covering six things:
Purpose.
A plain statement that hedging exists to reduce volatility in business outcomes, not to generate profit. This single sentence settles most later arguments.
Hedge ratio.
What proportion of exposure gets hedged, and over what horizon. Many companies hedge a high share of near-term committed exposures and a declining share of distant, less certain ones.
Permitted instruments.
An explicit list, usually plain forwards and simple options, with exotic structures either banned or requiring board approval.
Authority and segregation.
Who may transact, who confirms and records, and who reviews. The person placing a hedge should never be the only person tracking it.
Cash planning.
Exchange-traded hedges settle gains and losses daily, so a correct hedge can still demand cash midway. Liquidity for margin calls has to be planned before the hedge is placed.
Review basis.
Performance judged against the policy, not against hindsight. The right question is whether the rule was followed, not whether the rate later moved the other way.

body.title: The Founder With a Dollar Cloud Bill
body.scenario: You are the founder of a Bengaluru software company. All revenue is in rupees from Indian customers. Cloud hosting, payment gateway fees and a few software subscriptions cost about USD 40,000 a month and are rising with usage. The rupee has weakened about 5% over the past year, and your finance lead suggests starting to hedge. You have no treasury team and no derivatives experience.
body.prompt: Should you hedge, and if so how would you keep it simple and safe?
body.modelAnswer: First, size it honestly. USD 40,000 a month is about USD 4.8 lakh a year, so a 5% rupee move changes annual cost by roughly 5% of that, which in rupee terms is meaningful but is unlikely to be the largest risk in an early-stage software business. The purpose of hedging here is predictability of a growing cost line, not profit. Second, exhaust the free options before buying any instrument. Check whether your cloud provider offers rupee-denominated billing or an annual committed-use plan at a fixed rupee price, since that shifts the currency risk to them. Ask whether any customer contracts can be priced with a clause allowing revision if input costs rise. Consider whether you can win even a small amount of dollar revenue, from an overseas customer or a marketplace payout, because that is a natural hedge and costs nothing. Third, if you still want a hedge, keep it plain: a simple forward with your existing bank for the next three to six months of expected dollar payments, hedging perhaps half to two-thirds of that, and nothing beyond what you are confident you will actually spend. Avoid exchange-traded futures for now, because daily margin calls demand attention and cash you would rather put into the product, and avoid any structured product a bank offers with a cleverly discounted rate, since the discount is always paid for in a scenario you have not thought about. Fourth, write down three lines before you transact: what percentage you hedge, for how far ahead, and that the purpose is stability rather than gain. Finally, accept in advance that in roughly half of the periods the hedge will look like a mistake in hindsight. If that will bother your board, do not start hedging, because abandoning a policy mid-cycle is worse than never having one.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: The amount paid upfront to buy an option, which is the maximum the buyer can lose, is called the ___.
body.explanation: The premium is non-refundable. It buys a right, not an obligation, which is exactly what makes options suitable for exposures that may never materialise, such as a tender you might not win.

body.title: Before Your Company Places Any Hedge
steps: Write down the exposure in one line: what currency or commodity, how much, and on what date
Confirm the exposure is real and committed, and use options rather than forwards where it is only probable
Check for a natural hedge first, since matching inflows and outflows costs nothing
Decide the hedge ratio in advance, and record it, so nobody has to justify it in hindsight later
Stick to instruments you can explain in two sentences, and treat any structure offering a better than market rate as a warning sign
Plan the cash needed for margin calls if the hedge is exchange-traded
Separate the person who transacts from the person who records and reviews

cards.definition: A position taken to offset an existing business exposure, so gains on one side cancel losses on the other.
A customised agreement with a bank to transact at a rate fixed today for a future date. An obligation, with no upfront premium.
A standardised exchange-traded version of a forward, requiring margin and settling gains and losses daily.
The right to buy at a fixed strike price. Used to protect against a price or rate rising.
The right to sell at a fixed strike price. Used to protect against a price or rate falling.
The fixed price or rate at which an option can be exercised.
The upfront, non-refundable cost of buying an option, and the buyer's maximum loss.
The proportion of an exposure that is hedged, set by policy rather than decided case by case.
A structural offset within the business, such as earning and spending in the same foreign currency.
Daily revaluation of a position, with gains and losses settled in cash on exchange-traded contracts.

points: Hedging buys certainty, so a hedge that loses money while keeping outcomes predictable has done exactly what it was meant to do
A forward fixes a rate with your bank, removing both the downside and the upside, with no premium but a rate that embeds a cost
Futures do the same job through an exchange in standard lots, with margin and daily cash settlement
An option costs a premium upfront and gives a right rather than an obligation, which suits uncertain exposures such as a tender you may not win
For the worked example, the forward fixed the cost at ₹85.20 while the option capped the worst case at ₹86.20 and kept the benefit if the rupee strengthened
The natural hedge is always the cheapest, so match foreign currency inflows and outflows before buying any instrument
A position larger than the underlying exposure is a trade, not a hedge, and a written policy with a hedge ratio, permitted instruments and segregated authority is what keeps the difference clear

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not investment, trading, hedging or financial advice, and nothing here is a recommendation to transact in any derivative. All rates, premiums and outcomes used are simplified teaching examples that exclude brokerage, taxes, bank charges and documentation requirements. Permitted hedging instruments and underlying exposure requirements are governed by RBI and SEBI rules that change over time. Companies should take professional advice and follow a board-approved policy before using derivatives.
